title: Terragrunt and our infrastructure repo

story: You want to keep three lite VMs warm instead of two: one number in one file. But imagine the whole ai-agents account lives in one big OpenTofu folder with one state. Your plan refreshes every network rule, bucket, DNS record and role in the account, takes minutes, and shows a teammate's half-finished bucket change next to yours. While DevOps applies a network change, the state is locked and you cannot even plan. And the most worrying part: your small change and the network that every VM depends on sit in the same plan, so one wrong destroy line there takes every VM offline.

So the team splits the account into small folders, one per piece, each with its own state. That fixes the speed and the risk, but it creates new problems. Every folder now needs the same state settings and the same tags, copied twenty times. And the sandboxes folder needs the subnet IDs that only the network folder knows.
hook.question: How do we split infrastructure into small pieces without copying the same settings into each one, and still let one piece use what another piece created?

p: Terragrunt is a thin tool that sits in front of OpenTofu. It does not create anything itself: in each folder it prepares the files, then runs tofu there. Our infrastructure repo uses it to split every account into many small folders called units. A unit is a folder with one terragrunt.hcl file in it, which says which module to run and with which inputs. Each unit has its own state, so a plan in the sandboxes unit can only change the sandboxes. It cannot even see the network, so it cannot destroy it by mistake.

The folders are arranged by account, then cloud, then region, then piece. That path is not only tidy. It is also the name of each unit's state file, so two units can never share a state, even when they run the same module.

code.file: the lab's tree, which has the same shape as the real repo
code.text:
terraform/
├── root.hcl                   shared by every unit: where state goes, common inputs
└── accounts/ai-agents/
    ├── account.hcl            facts about this account: name prefix, tags
    └── aws/us-east-1/
        ├── core-services/
        │   ├── vpc/terragrunt.hcl          unit: the private network
        │   └── runs-bucket/terragrunt.hcl  unit: the bucket for run transcripts
        └── sandboxes/terragrunt.hcl        unit: launch templates and warm pools
modules/
├── vpc/       plain OpenTofu modules: the code each unit runs
├── pool/
└── bucket/

notes.text: root.hcl is at the top, so every unit below it can include it.
account.hcl holds what is true for every unit in one account.
A unit: one folder, one terragrunt.hcl, one state.
Modules are ordinary OpenTofu folders. A unit says which one to run; the module does not know about Terragrunt.

read.h: Write the shared parts once: include
p: Every unit starts with an include block that pulls in root.hcl. Whatever the root says, the unit gets, much like a tsconfig.json that extends a base config. find_in_parent_folders walks up the folders until it finds the file, so a unit does not need to know how deep it sits.

The root says two things. Its remote_state block says where state lives, and Terragrunt writes that into a backend.tf file before it runs tofu. The key part is path_relative_to_include(), which gives the unit's path from the root, so the vpc unit's state lands at accounts/ai-agents/aws/us-east-1/core-services/vpc/terraform.tfstate. Its inputs block passes values to every unit. Here those are the name prefix and the tags, read from the account.hcl of whichever account the unit lives in. In the lab the state is a local file; in the real repo the same block points at an S3 bucket with a lock.

notes.text: Find the nearest account.hcl above the unit and read its locals. A unit in another account would find that account's file.
get_parent_terragrunt_dir() is the folder of root.hcl; path_relative_to_include() is the unit's path below it. Every unit gets a different path.
Terragrunt writes the backend settings into backend.tf for each unit, so no unit repeats them.
Shared inputs. A unit's own inputs are merged on top of these.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the // in the source
p: A unit's source looks like "<path>/..//modules/vpc". Terragrunt copies everything before the double slash into a cache folder, .terragrunt-cache, and runs tofu in the part after it. Copying the whole folder means a module can still reach its neighbours with ../, for example a shared template.

Inputs reach OpenTofu as environment variables (TF_VAR_name_prefix and so on). A module simply ignores inputs it does not declare, so the root can pass name_prefix to every unit, even to a module that has no use for it.

The sandboxes need the subnet IDs, and only the vpc unit knows them, because they are its outputs. A dependency block connects the two. Terragrunt runs tofu output in the vpc unit, reads private_subnets, and passes it to the sandboxes as an input. The same block also sets the order: the vpc unit must exist before the sandboxes.

There is a problem on the very first plan, when the vpc unit has never been applied. It has no state, so it has no outputs to read. mock_outputs solves this with stand-in values, so that plan and validate can still run. The line under it allows the mocks for validate and plan only, so an apply can never build anything on fake subnets: it fails until the vpc unit really exists. You can see them in the plan below: the sandboxes plan shows 10.0.0.0/18, the mock, while the vpc plan shows the real 10.60.x subnets it is about to create.

terragrunt run --all runs one tofu command in every unit below the folder you are in, in dependency order. For plan that is safe and useful. For apply it asks one question, then applies every unit without showing you each plan, which is why in our repo a person applies after reading each unit's plan.

notes.text: The same include as every unit: state settings and shared inputs come from the root.
Run the pool module from the modules/ folder next to terraform/.
The unit this one depends on, as a relative path.
Stand-in outputs, used only while the vpc unit has no state yet.
Mocks are allowed for validate and plan only. An apply without real outputs fails instead of using fake subnets.
dependency.<name>.outputs.<output>: the vpc unit's real output once it exists.

read.see:
$ terragrunt run --all plan
The following units will be run, starting with dependencies and then their dependents:
╰── core-services/vpc
    ╰── sandboxes
[core-services/vpc] tofu: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
WARN [sandboxes] ... has no outputs, but mock outputs provided and returning those in dependency output.
[sandboxes] tofu:               + "10.0.0.0/18",
[sandboxes] tofu: Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

deeper.h: Go deeper: two trees and the n8n pattern
p: Our repo has two trees. The new one starts at terraform/root.hcl and is arranged as accounts/<account>/<cloud>/<region or global>/<piece>, exactly like the lab. New AWS accounts, including the ai-agents account, go there.

The old tree starts at a root.hcl at the top of the repo, under multi_tenant/accounts/<account>/<piece>/. Tools that run on our internal Kubernetes cluster live there, in multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/. n8n, an older workflow tool, is the model to copy: one folder per tool, with one unit per piece (iam, secrets, rds, sg, s3 and repository, which installs the Helm chart), plus an n8n.hcl file with the facts they share. Lesson p5-2 walks through that pattern.

lab.title: A small ai-agents tree with Terragrunt
needs: Terragrunt 1.0 or newer (terragrunt --version). It uses tofu when Terraform is not installed.
No cloud account: every module only stores values, like the warm pool record in p4-1.
lab.goal: Build a small copy of the ai-agents tree with a shared root, two units and a dependency, and see each unit get its own state and the shared inputs.

guess.q: Both units include the same root.hcl. The vpc unit is at accounts/ai-agents/aws/us-east-1/core-services/vpc and the sandboxes unit at accounts/ai-agents/aws/us-east-1/sandboxes. How many state files will exist after you apply both?

options.text: One, because both units include the same root.hcl, which has one remote_state block.
options.why: The block is shared, but the path inside it uses path_relative_to_include(), which is different for every unit.

options.text: Two, one per unit, each at a path named after the unit's folder.
options.why: The root writes one backend.tf per unit, and each one points at accounts/.../<unit>/terraform.tfstate. Shared settings, separate states.

options.text: Three: one for each unit and one for the root.
options.why: The root is not a unit. It never runs tofu itself; it only gives settings to the units that include it.

follow.say: Make the lab folder and paste this block, because it writes three tiny modules for you: a VPC, a pool and a bucket that only store values. The Terragrunt files are the lesson, so you write those yourself next.

Save the four Terragrunt files: root.hcl and the sandboxes unit from the Understand step, plus account.hcl and the vpc unit below. Put each one at the path in its first line, because Terragrunt finds them by folder.
Ask Terragrunt in which order it would run the units, because the dependency block should put vpc first.
Look at the sandboxes unit the way OpenTofu will receive it, with the root's inputs merged in, because that is the include working.
Plan every unit at once. The vpc has never been applied, so watch the sandboxes plan use the mock subnet.
follow.see:
[core-services/vpc] tofu:           + cidr = "10.60.0.0/16"
[core-services/vpc] tofu: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
[core-services/vpc] tofu:       + "10.60.0.0/18",
…
WARN   [sandboxes] Config …/core-services/vpc/terragrunt.hcl is a dependency of …/sandboxes/terragrunt.hcl that has no outputs, but mock outputs provided and returning those in dependency output.
[sandboxes] tofu:               + "10.0.0.0/18",
[sandboxes] tofu: Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

follow.say: Apply both in order and answer y. This is a lab on your laptop; in the real repo nobody runs run --all apply on an account, because one y would apply every unit without showing each plan.
follow.do: terragrunt run --all apply 2>&1 | grep -E 'Are you sure|Apply complete|sandboxes.*"10\.'
follow.see:
Are you sure you want to run 'terragrunt apply' in each unit of the run queue displayed above? (y/n) y
[core-services/vpc] tofu: Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
[sandboxes] tofu:               + "10.60.0.0/18",
[sandboxes] tofu:               + "10.60.64.0/18",
[sandboxes] tofu:               + "10.60.128.0/18",
[sandboxes] tofu: Apply complete! Resources: 2 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

follow.say: Find the state files, because the folder paths are the proof that every unit has a state of its own.

lab.build: Add a third unit, core-services/runs-bucket, for the bucket where runs keep their transcripts. Its module is modules/bucket, which needs bucket_name and tags. Give it bucket_name = "rhino-ai-agents-runs" and let the tags come from the root. Before you apply, predict where its state file will appear. Then run terragrunt list --dag, terragrunt run --all plan and terragrunt run --all apply.
checks: terragrunt list --dag shows three units: core-services/runs-bucket, core-services/vpc and sandboxes.
terragrunt render in the runs-bucket folder shows bucket_name = "rhino-ai-agents-runs" and the tags with account_name = "ai-agents", which you did not write in the unit.
run --all plan says Plan: 1 to add for runs-bucket and No changes for vpc and sandboxes.
A third state file exists at terraform/.state/accounts/ai-agents/aws/us-east-1/core-services/runs-bucket/terraform.tfstate.
Your new terragrunt.hcl has no remote_state block and no tags of its own: both come from the root.
lab.fix: A teammate wants Spot groups next to the normal ones, so they copy the sandboxes folder to sandboxes-spot. They delete the include block ("every unit has the same lines anyway"), and when the source path stops working they write it out by hand as "../../../../../..//modules/pool". Now terragrunt plan in sandboxes-spot stops and asks for var.name_prefix, then var.tags. Press Ctrl+C. Find what is missing and put it back, using the sandboxes unit as your model. Then explain one more problem the copy had that no error showed: where would its state have been written without the root's remote_state block? (Look inside .terragrunt-cache.)
explain: Why does every unit get its own state file, even though they all include the same root.hcl?
What does the dependency block give the sandboxes unit, and why does the first plan need mock_outputs?
Why is terragrunt run --all plan a normal thing to run, but run --all apply on a real account is not?
lab.done: Three units plan and apply in dependency order, each with its own state file under terraform/.state, and the runs-bucket unit gets its tags from the root.

check.q: The vpc unit and the sandboxes unit include the same root.hcl. You apply the sandboxes unit. Can that apply destroy the VPC?

options.text: Yes, because both units share the root's state settings.
options.why: They share the settings, but path_relative_to_include() gives each unit its own state file. The sandboxes state does not contain the VPC.

options.text: No. The sandboxes apply only knows the resources in its own state and configuration, and the VPC is in neither.
options.why: That is the point of small units: a plan or apply can only touch what its own state and configuration describe.

options.text: Only if the sandboxes unit has a dependency block on the vpc unit.
options.why: A dependency only reads the vpc unit's outputs. It does not put the VPC's resources into the sandboxes state.

check.q: The vpc unit has never been applied, and the sandboxes unit reads dependency.vpc.outputs.private_subnets. What happens when you plan the sandboxes unit?

options.text: Terragrunt applies the vpc unit first, so that the outputs exist.
options.why: Plan never applies anything, not even a dependency. That would be a terrible surprise.

options.text: The plan fails, because there is no way to plan before the dependency exists.
options.why: That is what happens without mock_outputs. With them, plan can still run.

options.text: The plan uses the mock_outputs values, and apply would refuse to use them.
options.why: Mock outputs exist so that plan and validate work on a fresh account. Once the vpc unit is applied, its real outputs replace them.

check.q: A teammate copies a unit folder and deletes the include block because "every unit has the same lines anyway". What did the include give the unit?

options.text: Where its state lives (remote_state) and the shared inputs, such as the name prefix and the tags.
options.why: Without it, the module asks for name_prefix and tags, and even if you typed them, the state would land inside the cache folder instead of next to the other units' states.

options.text: Only the formatting rules for the file.
options.why: Formatting is checked by terragrunt hcl format. The include carries the state settings and shared inputs.

options.text: Nothing important, because the module path is enough to plan.
options.why: The module path says which code to run, not where its state lives or which shared inputs it receives.

p: RhinoHealth/infrastructure runs OpenTofu 1.12.6 with Terragrunt 1.1.4. The ai-agents account goes into the new tree at terraform/accounts/ai-agents/, copied from the solutions account, with units such as aws/us-east-1/core-services/vpc, core-services/runs-bucket, core-services/dns-firewall and sandboxes. The real root.hcl keeps state in the S3 bucket rhinohealth-terraform-state with the key ${path_relative_to_include()}/terraform.tfstate and use_lockfile = true, pins provider versions in common.hcl (for example aws 6.64.0), and makes every unit assume the account's TerraformDeploymentRole. Module sources in the new tree use "${get_parent_terragrunt_dir("root")}/..//modules/<name>/", and registry modules use tfr:/// with a pinned version.

The agents' Temporal and services run on the internal cluster, so they follow the n8n pattern in the old tree, under multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/ai-agents/. The infrastructure repo's CI only checks formatting today; plans are run on a laptop over VPN, pasted into the PR, and a person applies.

tickets.why: Adds terraform/accounts/ai-agents/ with account.hcl and the region files, copied from the solutions account.
The core-services units of the sandbox network: vpc, runs-bucket, dns-firewall and private-zone.
Temporal on the internal cluster, built as units in the old tree on the n8n pattern.
The agent services as more units in that folder, plus the PrivateLink unit.

words.plain: A thin tool in front of OpenTofu that prepares each folder's settings and runs tofu there, one folder at a time or all in order.
One folder with a terragrunt.hcl: one module, its inputs and its own state.
A block that pulls a parent file such as root.hcl into a unit, so shared settings are written once.
A block that reads another unit's outputs and makes that unit run first.
Stand-in outputs a dependency gives during plan and validate, before the other unit has ever been applied.
Runs one tofu command in every unit below the current folder, in dependency order.

review.q: Without looking: what two things does our root.hcl give every unit, and which function makes the state paths different?
review.a: The remote_state settings (where and how state is stored, written into backend.tf) and the shared inputs (name prefix, tags). path_relative_to_include() makes each unit's state key its own folder path.

review.q: You add a dns-firewall unit that needs the VPC ID. What do you write, and what happens on the first plan in a new account?
review.a: A dependency "vpc" block with config_path to the vpc unit and mock_outputs for vpc_id, then inputs = { vpc_id = dependency.vpc.outputs.vpc_id }. On the first plan the mock value is used; apply needs the real output, so the vpc unit is applied first.

review.q: Why would a team rather have twenty small units than one big folder for an account?
review.a: Faster plans, separate locks so people do not block each other, and a smaller blast radius: a mistake in one unit cannot destroy what another unit manages.

remember: One folder is one unit with one state; the root is written once and included everywhere, and a dependency passes outputs and sets the order.
